planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall into lean, sharply drained soil; unlike most daphnes, genkwa tolerates and even prefers more sun.

directions: Give lilac daphne full sun to very light shade and soil that drains quickly year-round, since wet roots are its main cause of failure. In early to mid-spring, clusters of lilac-blue to lavender flowers wreathe the bare, wiry stems before the foliage emerges, producing a soft haze of color and light fragrance unusual among daphnes for its violet rather than pink or white tone. It is slow to establish and resents being moved once planted, so choose a permanent well-drained site from the start and avoid disturbing the root zone. All parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered spot in humus-rich, well-drained soil; this is one of the larger, more upright daphnes and eventually needs room to develop into a small tree-like shrub.

directions: Site Jacqueline Postill in a sheltered spot with humus-rich, well-drained soil and protection from harsh winter wind, which can damage its largely evergreen foliage. From midwinter into early spring it opens clusters of rich pink-flushed white flowers with an extraordinarily powerful, carrying fragrance, making it prized near entries and windows where its scent can be enjoyed even from indoors. It grows taller and more upright than most garden daphnes, eventually forming a large multi-stemmed shrub, and like its relatives resents root disturbance once established. All parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; trailing stems root naturally where they touch the ground, so top-dress lightly with gritty compost to encourage the mat to spread.

directions: Blagayana forms a low, sprawling mat of trailing woody stems that root naturally as they creep across the ground, gradually layering themselves into a wider colony over time. In early spring, dense terminal clusters of creamy white flowers with an intense sweet fragrance appear at the branch tips, held close to the evergreen foliage. It prefers part shade with cool, humus-rich, sharply drained soil, and benefits from a light covering of leaf litter or grit over the trailing stems to encourage rooting. Avoid disturbing the root zone once established; all parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade; Manten is a compact hybrid that reblooms sporadically through the season rather than flowering once in spring.

directions: Manten forms a dense, rounded evergreen mound bearing reddish-purple, intensely fragrant flowers in a strong mid-spring flush, with lighter sporadic rebloom continuing into summer and fall. Awarded the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its combination of compact habit, glossy foliage, and unusually long bloom season for a daphne, it suits a shaded border edge or entry planting where repeat fragrance is valued. Give it humus-rich, sharply drained soil and avoid transplanting once established, since like other daphnes it resents root disturbance. All parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant in a raised bed or rock garden with sharp drainage and mulch with gravel rather than organic matter to keep the crown dry.

directions: Eximia is a selected form of rose daphne chosen for larger, deeper crimson-pink flower clusters and darker green foliage than the straight species, smothering its low, trailing evergreen mat in intensely fragrant bloom each late spring. It is a classic choice for rock gardens and raised beds, where its draping habit shows off well over stone and its scent carries across the whole planting. Sharp drainage is essential, since more plants are lost to wet, heavy soil than to cold; mulch with gravel rather than organic material to keep the crown dry. Avoid moving it once established, and note that all parts are toxic if ingested.
